The Six Rules, Recapped

  1. Add stops — /p t k/
  2. Voiceless before voiced obstruents (stops, fricatives, affricates)
  3. Add /s/
  4. Add nasals — /m n/
  5. Add liquids — /r l/ (though some languages just have one)
  6. Last priority: add glides — /w j/

Filling the Gaps

  • /k/, /s/, /m n/, and /r l/ are already covered by the names
  • Still missing: /p/ and /t/ (rules 1–2), and the glides /w j/ (rule 6)
  • Also strange: there’s only one voiceless/voiced pair (t/d)

What Changed

  • Postalveolar and retroflex merged — they sounded too similar to keep separate
  • Stop pairs got filled in systematically; voiced /d/ dropped
  • Unused columns got dropped so the chart reads cleanly

Now Check Your Own

Pull out the inventory you built from your name’s consonants + your three chosen sounds.

Checklist

  • Did you add the consonants from your names?
  • Did you add your three non-English consonants?
  • Does your C inventory follow the six “rules”?
  • Is your system balanced?

That said…

It’s fine to have some weirdness in your language!

But there is a limit:

  1. no stops
  2. has a bunch of fricatives, but no /s/
  3. nasals and stops not occurring at the same place of articulation
  4. no alveolars (or dentals) at all

Group Check

  • Trade charts with a groupmate
  • Have them examine your consonant chart:
    • anything ‘imbalanced’?
    • can they pronounce all of the sounds?

Vowels

What Makes a Consonant

Consonants involve at least one real point of obstruction — a full or partial closure somewhere in the vocal tract.

What Makes a Vowel

Vowels involve no closure at all — an open vocal tract, shaped by the tongue and lips into different resonating cavities.

Real-Time MRI of Spoken Language

  • How are Vowels Made?

The Classic IPA “Trapezoid”

Oral Cavity > “Trapezoid”

  • Front of the mouth (lips/teeth) is on the left; back of the throat (pharynx) is on the right
  • The tongue body rises toward the palate for high vowels, drops toward the jaw for low ones

Moving the Tongue Around: Height & Frontness

Height

The vertical position of the tongue body in the mouth.

  • High: tongue raised close to the roof of the mouth — [i] as in beet
  • Mid: in between — [ɛ] as in bet
  • Low: tongue low, jaw dropped — [æ] as in bat

Frontness

The horizontal position of the tongue body.

  • Front: tongue bunched toward the front — [i] as in beet
  • Central: neither — [ʌ] as in but
  • Back: tongue pulled toward the back — [u] as in boot

Do you notice anything else changing besides tongue placement?

beet ~ boot

bait ~ boat

Roundedness

  • Rounded: lips protruded/rounded — [u] as in boot
  • Unrounded: lips spread or neutral — [i] as in beet

Tenseness

  • Tense: produced with more muscular tension, often slightly longer — [i] as in beet
  • Lax: more relaxed, often shorter — [ɪ] as in bit
  • Tenseness pairs vowels at a similar height: i/ɪ, e/ɛ, u/ʊ, o/ɔ

Consonant Features

  1. Place
  2. Manner
  3. Voicing

Vowel Features

  1. Height
  2. Frontness
  3. Roundedness
  4. Tenseness
